  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark

Vignette:
Nadia’s memory of the convoy patrol during her tour did not unfold in scenes, but in a single, unbroken stretch of panic. It was late October, the sky already bruising toward dark, when the road ahead dissolved in a wall of heat and shrapnel. The radio commands had been sudden, forcing her legs into a sprint that burned her lungs and made her knees buckle on the uneven terrain. She had run until her chest hitched, until the ground tilted beneath her boots, until the static drowned out everything but the thudding of her own pulse. When she finally collapsed behind a concrete barrier, the darkness had already swallowed the landscape, leaving her certain she could not see the full extent of the damage or who was still moving in the shadows. Returning to civilian life, Nadia found her body had become a landscape of warnings. She was certain that any sustained effort would push her past a point of no return. When the fire alarm tested at her apartment complex, she took the building’s service elevator even on the fourth floor, refusing to let her heart climb. She stopped accepting weekend invitations that required hiking or dancing, citing fatigue, though it was really the dread of feeling her breath grow short in crowded rooms. Her commute shifted from a brisk walk to a parked car at the far edge of the garage, and she began tracking every minor ache as if it were a countdown. Parallel to this physical caution, she had come to believe that disorder was a precursor to collapse. In her apartment, she began scrubbing the kitchen tiles until her knuckles grew raw, reorganizing the pantry three times in a week, and aligning every chair to the exact millimeter. At work, where she managed large clinical datasets as a database administrator, the compulsion manifested in quiet repetitions. She would rerun the same query logs, cross-checking entries until the spreadsheet cells were perfectly color-coded, pausing only to wipe her desk down with a microfiber cloth. Her supervisor noticed the extra hours but misread them as diligence, not as Nadia’s insistence that if she could just map every variable and purge every error, she could rebuild the order the world had stolen from her. Nightfall brought its own particular weight. Nadia had come to believe that once the sun dropped, the environment turned hostile and untrackable. She locked her apartment doors twice, drew the blinds, and declined plans that extended past six o’clock. When her sister mentioned an evening gallery opening, Nadia cited work deadlines, though her hands had already started trembling at the thought of walking past streetlights or navigating unfamiliar crowds in the dark. She began taking different grocery routes, sticking to brightly lit aisles, and leaving immediately when her shift ended, refusing to linger in parking lots where shadows pooled. The cumulative weight of these habits had quietly carved her life smaller. Her phone rarely rang after dark. Her exercise routine gathered dust. She told herself she was merely prioritizing stability, but the constant scanning and the rigid routines left her exhausted before dawn. What finally brought her to the clinic was not a single crisis, but a Tuesday morning when she stood in her office bathroom, staring at a database migration log that refused to sync, and felt her legs give out beneath her. The memory arrived without warning, a sudden flash of heat and radio chatter that made her drop her stylus and press her palms flat against her thighs until her breathing steadied. She realized she could no longer rely on her own systems to keep her grounded. She was afraid the physical toll would finally fracture, but she was also hoping to learn how to stop bracing for a threat that no longer occupied the space beside her.
